stories.topic: India's Founding Leaders Ran Cities First
stories.summary: Amit points out that under British rule India had genuinely empowered municipal leaders. C. Rajagopalachari was effectively mayor of Salem in 1917 as chairman of the municipal board. Jawaharlal Nehru held a similar post in Allahabad in 1923. Chittaranjan Das and later Subhas Chandra Bose held it in Calcutta, and Sardar Patel was prominent in municipal politics. The colonial government couldn't be bothered with local tasks, so these bodies had real power, and they became a training ground for the men who later ran independent India.
stories.insight: The founders were not activists who walked straight into government. They learned governance and public finance by running cities. Independent India kept the colonial coercive superstructure and lost this local layer, which was the part that worked.
stories.quote: So it is not exactly true that all of these great leaders, some of whom you know were actually a prime minister and home minister when we got independence, that they just went from being activists to politicians. It wasn't like that at all. They knew governance, they cared deeply about it, they understood public finance.

stories.topic: Latin America to Africa, Inside One Country
stories.summary: Years ago Lant Pritchett told Ajay about a comparison he had been working on. Divide the richest place in Latin America by the poorest place in Africa, and you get roughly the same ratio as the richest place in India divided by the poorest place in India.
stories.insight: India's internal spread is as wide as the gap between continents. That is why heterogeneity has to be a first-order consideration in every question about policy, about the state, and even about how firms are designed.
stories.quote: The ratio of the richest place in Latin America divided by the poorest place in Africa is the kind of number that you get with the richest place in India divided by the poorest place in India. India is that diverse and that heterogeneous.

stories.summary: Using figures from Nilakantan RS's book South vs North, Amit compares states. Kerala's life expectancy is 75, like Argentina or Thailand. Uttar Pradesh's is 64, like Liberia, Ethiopia or Haiti. Kerala's infant mortality is 7 per thousand, close to the USA's 6. Tamil Nadu is at 15, middling states like Punjab and Maharashtra are around 19 to 20, and Madhya Pradesh is at 48. The health problems differ too: Kerala struggles with diabetes and obesity, while the heartland struggles with malnutrition and stunting.
stories.insight: These are different countries sharing one flag. A centrally designed health policy will be wrong for at least one of them, and Keralites handed a malnutrition programme will rightly ask why.
stories.quote: So you have Kerala at seven and you have Madhya Pradesh at forty eight, which just completely blows my mind.

stories.topic: Uttar Pradesh Is France, Germany, Italy and Spain Combined
stories.summary: Drawing on his conversations with Karthik Muralidharan, Amit notes that India's fifteen biggest states would all rank among the world's top 42 countries by population. By his own calculation, Uttar Pradesh has as many people as France, Germany, Italy and Spain put together. Karthik also points out that the average Indian district is bigger than 85 countries, yet a district has no real democracy of its own because everything is decided above it.
stories.insight: Calling UP 'a state' hides a governance load that four major European nations share between them. Given the scale, it is no surprise so much goes wrong.
stories.quote: Uttar Pradesh is the size of France, Germany, Italy and Spain combined. Right, it is that big.

stories.topic: China Is More Decentralized Than India
stories.summary: Citing Karthik Muralidharan's book and their latest conversation, Amit says only about 3% of India's budget is spent at the local level. In China, which we think of as highly centralized, about 50% is spent locally, and local authorities have wide powers to act.
stories.insight: The common picture is the wrong way round. On the measure that matters, which is who controls the money, India is far more centralized than the country it imagines as the model of central control.
stories.quote: three percent of India's budget is spent at the local level. And in China, which we think of as so centralized, fifty percent is spent at the local level.

stories.topic: Rising Divorce Rates as a Sign of Empowerment
stories.summary: Ajay had described young women's mobile phone ownership as a measure of empowerment. Amit added his own unconventional metric from a column he wrote more than a decade ago: rising divorce rates. Where others lamented that India was 'becoming like the West', he saw women gaining the independence to leave bad marriages. In his Seen and the Unseen episode Metrics of Empowerment, his guests proposed others, such as who in the household orders the groceries.
stories.insight: Good metrics are often the ones that cause unease. A number society treats as decline can be a sign of rising agency once you ask what it actually measures.
stories.quote: my point was that rising divorce rates means more women are getting empowered and have the agency and perhaps the independence to walk away from bad marriages.

stories.topic: Kerala Was Three Steps Ahead on COVID
stories.summary: Malayali students returning from China brought COVID back early, so Kerala faced the first wave before almost anyone else in India. Its capable health system was already running quarantines and isolation. Meanwhile the Union government first did nothing, then imposed uniform nationwide lockdowns. Kerala's health authorities pushed back, saying they knew what they were doing.
stories.insight: Once a state has built real capability, instructions from New Delhi make things worse, not better. Decisions should rest with whoever holds the local knowledge.
stories.quote: We know what to do. Don't tell us what to do. We are probably three steps ahead of you.

stories.topic: Susan Thomas and the Dog Bite in Kerala
stories.summary: Susan Thomas was bitten by a family dog in Kerala. She insists it was her fault for troubling the dog. Three things surprised Ajay. The family took her to a government clinic without a second thought. The doctor was present and competent. And he asked the right questions: was it a family dog, was it fine, would it stay under observation? Since the answers were yes, he gave her antiseptic and sent her home. Rabies vaccination would start only if the dog showed symptoms. In most of India, Ajay says, the family would go private, the government clinic would be empty or staffed by someone unqualified, and the patient would get nine rabies injections.
stories.insight: Ajay wants radical reform of most of India's government health systems, but he respects Kerala's. One small encounter shows why a single national prescription cannot fit both.
stories.quote: Because if the dog has rabies, the dog will collapse and go crazy first. That time we start the rabies vaccinations for the human.

stories.summary: The Kerala doctor's restraint reminded Amit of Lancelot Pinto, who treated him through COVID twice. Pinto's view was that many COVID deaths came from over-medication. Patients demanded aggressive drugs, their immune systems overreacted, and they died a week later from the treatment rather than the virus. Pinto began with paracetamol and stepped up only when needed. Amit never needed anything beyond paracetamol and cough syrup.
stories.insight: Good medicine sometimes means going against the protocol a doctor can hide behind. Restraint takes courage, because if a patient dies anyway the doctor who didn't play by the book gets the blame.
stories.quote: it was a structured approach and not play by the book, which is especially courageous because playing by the book is a safe thing to do.

stories.topic: The Netherlands Hands Its Tanks to Germany
stories.summary: After the Second World War the Netherlands forgave Germany and went back to buying German tanks. With only a handful of tanks, the logistics, maintenance and management needed to run them was hopelessly small-scale. So the Dutch made a deal: they would keep paying for the tanks, but the German army would command them, with Dutch soldiers serving inside fully integrated German units.
stories.insight: This is the European approach to federalism: decide each function at the scale that makes sense, instead of assuming every country must do everything inside its own borders.
stories.quote: We'll pay for the tanks, but the tanks will be controlled by the German army on our behalf.

stories.topic: The Catholic Church's Secret Was Subsidiarity
stories.summary: Economists repeat the subsidiarity principle as if it were theirs, but Ajay traces it to the Catholic Church. From around 380 to about 1950 the Church was a major world power. It controlled armies, joined international treaties, and lasted longer than most empires. Its design secret was decentralization: churches everywhere had their own autonomy, and central control was kept to a minimum.
stories.insight: Empires tended to collapse partly because they centralized. The organization that lasted longest did the opposite, so subsidiarity is a proven survival strategy and not just a theory.
stories.quote: They lived longer than most empires. Empires tended to crash partly because empires did more centralizing. And one of the design secrets of the Catholic Church was decentralization.

stories.topic: The Fable of the Monkey and the Two Cats
stories.summary: Amit retells a fable from a Pranay Kotasthane newsletter post. Two cats fight over a piece of bread, and a monkey offers to divide it fairly. Each time one half is bigger, he takes a bite to even it out, until only two crumbs are left. He then eats those as payment for his work. Pranay's point is that India argues endlessly about horizontal devolution, meaning which state gets how much. It barely discusses vertical devolution, meaning how much money the centre passes down at all. Only 42% goes to the states.
stories.insight: While the states quarrel over shares, the centre keeps most of the money. The bigger decentralization question is the size of the total that leaves New Delhi, not how it is split.
stories.quote: But hey, I put in so much labor doing this, I need to be paid for my efforts

recommendations.item: Lant Pritchett Is on Team Prosperity (Episode 379 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lant Pritchett
recommendations.context: The episode opens with an idea that came to Amit while researching this conversation: nation-states and city governments evolved in opposite ways.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls Pritchett a great economist and 'such a great man that no amount of time would have done it justice.' His work started the line of thinking behind this episode.

recommendations.item: CMIE Consumer Pyramids dx
recommendations.creator: CMIE
recommendations.context: Ajay's preferred household survey data, which splits India into about 100 homogeneous regions of roughly seven districts each.
recommendations.reason: It lets you measure India's internal gaps: about 5x in income between the richest and poorest regions, and 10-15x in young women's mobile phone ownership.

recommendations.item: From Imperial to Adaptive Firms (Episode 37 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay links Indian heterogeneity back to this earlier episode.
recommendations.reason: It makes the same point for business that this episode makes for government. One design works across a homogeneous country like Germany, but firms in India have to build in the information and incentives to handle huge diversity.

recommendations.item: Metrics of Empowerment (Episode 88 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Devika Kher, Nidhi Gupta and Hamsini Hariharan
recommendations.context: Ajay's women-and-mobile-phones metric reminded Amit of this episode.
recommendations.reason: Three thinkers Amit calls phenomenal come up with unconventional measures of women's empowerment, such as who in the house orders the groceries.

recommendations.item: We Should Celebrate Rising Divorce Rates
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: His controversial column from more than a decade ago, mentioned during the discussion of empowerment metrics.
recommendations.reason: It argues that rising divorce rates show women gaining the agency and independence to leave bad marriages, which is progress, not decline.

recommendations.item: South vs North
recommendations.creator: Nilakantan RS
recommendations.context: The source of Amit's state-level figures on life expectancy, infant mortality, and Kerala's diabetes versus the heartland's malnutrition.
recommendations.reason: It sets out in hard numbers how different Indian states are, and why one central policy fails them.

recommendations.item: South India Would Like to Have a Word (Episode 320 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Nilakantan RS
recommendations.context: Mentioned while Amit cites Nilakantan's book.
recommendations.reason: A long conversation with the author whose data underpins the north-south comparisons in this episode.

recommendations.item: Accelerating India's Development
recommendations.creator: Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.context: Karthik's newly released book, cited for the scale of Indian states and districts and for local-level spending.
recommendations.reason: It is the source of eye-opening comparisons: the average district is bigger than 85 countries, and India spends about 3% of its budget locally against China's 50%.

recommendations.item: Karthik Muralidharan Examines the Indian State (Episode 290 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.context: One of four conversations Amit recorded with Karthik, which taught him about the sheer size of Indian states.
recommendations.reason: A deep look at how the Indian state works and why governing at this scale is so hard.

recommendations.item: Karthik Muralidharan and the Bureaucrat's Burden (Episode 375 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
recommendations.context: Their latest conversation, where the gap between India's and China's local spending comes up.
recommendations.reason: It continues the argument about state capacity and how little power and money India gives its local governments.

recommendations.item: The Practice of Medicine (Episode 229 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Lancelot Pinto
recommendations.context: A side note after Ajay's story about the Kerala doctor's sensible treatment.
recommendations.reason: Pinto, whom Amit calls one of the great doctors in the country, explains why he avoids over-medicating and takes a structured approach, including in treating COVID.

recommendations.item: Brave New World
recommendations.creator: Vasant Dhar
recommendations.context: Mentioned just before Amit tells Vasant Dhar's story about his friend Bubba.
recommendations.reason: Amit produces the show and calls it 'a great podcast', so check that out.

recommendations.item: The Fable of the Monkey and the Two Cats
recommendations.creator: Pranay Kotasthane
recommendations.context: Amit calls it a 'great newsletter post' and retells it to frame India's fiscal federalism.
recommendations.reason: It uses a simple fable to show that India obsesses over how money is divided among states and ignores how little the centre hands down in the first place.

recommendations.item: Centrally Sponsored Government Schemes (Episode 17 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Pranay Kotasthane
recommendations.context: Mentioned when Ajay argues that centrally sponsored schemes should be abolished.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it 'a great episode' in which Pranay made the same argument about seven years earlier.

recommendations.item: Shruti Rajagopalan on India's many constitutional amendments
recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: A recorded talk Amit calls 'a must watch' after Ajay mentions parties having the numbers to amend the Constitution.
recommendations.reason: It shows how Nehru started a habit of amending the Constitution whenever he wanted to do something unconstitutional, and how routine that habit became.

recommendations.item: Urban Governance in India (Episode 31 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: A short early episode Amit recalls during the discussion of city governance.
recommendations.reason: Shruti explains why Indian cities are badly run: power and accountability are not linked.

recommendations.item: Exit, Voice, and Loyalty
recommendations.creator: Albert O Hirschman
recommendations.context: Ajay cites 'the great Hirschman book' to explain how American federalism relies on migration.
recommendations.reason: It gives the framework for seeing migration as 'exit': Indians are used to loyalty or a little voice, while Americans simply move when their city or state fails them.

recommendations.item: Seeing Like a State
recommendations.creator: James C Scott
recommendations.context: Ajay draws on James C. Scott's ideas about early states, and the show notes link this book.
recommendations.reason: Scott's point that early states competed for people rather than land supports Ajay's case for celebrating migration.

recommendations.item: Our Population Is Our Greatest Asset (Episode 20 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay refers back to the end of this episode, where he raised India's demographic transition.
recommendations.reason: It explains why low-fertility states will need migrants, which ties population change to decentralization.

recommendations.item: The Power Broker
recommendations.creator: Robert Caro
recommendations.context: Named in Amit's closing recommendation as a book he would naturally recommend and has recommended before.
recommendations.reason: Its central character, Robert Moses, stands for the top-down approach to cities that Jane Jacobs fought.

recommendations.item: Triumph of the City
recommendations.creator: Edward Glaeser
recommendations.context: Named alongside The Power Broker in Amit's closing recommendation.
recommendations.reason: Amit considers it essential reading on cities and has recommended it on the show before.

recommendations.item: The Death and Life of Great American Cities
recommendations.creator: Jane Jacobs
recommendations.context: Amit's main recommendation for this episode.
recommendations.reason: He calls it 'an absolute masterpiece'. Jacobs argues that cities grow from the bottom up and are made of people more than buildings and highways. Amit ranks her among the great thinkers of the twentieth century, and says anyone living in a city has skin in the game.

recommendations.item: Bimal Patel's forthcoming book
recommendations.creator: Bimal Patel
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation is a book that isn't out yet, which he reveals as a secret. Amit also endorses Patel.
recommendations.reason: Ajay calls Patel India's preeminent urban thinker, someone who 'gets town planning in a way that essentially nobody in India does.' When the book comes out, 'run, not walk'.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay cites his book with Kelkar while explaining why concentrated power at the state level worries him.
recommendations.reason: It argues that economic development is at heart about dispersing power and building checks and balances, which is the idea underneath the whole decentralization debate.

core_ideas.concept: Nation-States Were Built Top-Down, Cities Bottom-Up
core_ideas.explanation: Nation-states began as coercive structures. They wanted tax revenue and conscripts for war and gave little in return. City governments grew out of need: once enough people lived together, they required order, rule of law and basic services, so city government was naturally responsive. India inherited the coercive nation-state and never let responsive government grow from below.
core_ideas.quote: what we have kind of landed up in India with is essentially just the larger coercive superstructure of the nation state with no concept of what a truly responsive government is.

core_ideas.explanation: India's 3.3 million square kilometres differ in culture, food and above all economics. Across CMIE's roughly 100 homogeneous regions, average income varies about 5x. Young women's mobile phone ownership varies 10-15x, from 90-95% in the best regions to 5-15% in the worst. A gap this large should shape every policy question.
core_ideas.quote: So just think that the mobile phone ownership of the best places is like 90%, 95%, and the worst places are like 5%, 10%, 15%.

core_ideas.concept: Place Changes Both What the State Should Do and How
core_ideas.explanation: The problems that need public action differ by place: air quality in the north, Arabian Sea cyclones and rising waters in Kerala. How to tackle them should differ too, including technology, organizational design and pay. India pays civil servants roughly the same everywhere, so they are underpaid in rich places and overpaid in poor ones, which distorts the whole state.
core_ideas.quote: A civil servant in Bombay should get paid more than a civil servant living in Calcutta.

core_ideas.concept: Mosquitoes Can Be Beaten, but Only Locally
core_ideas.explanation: Indians have largely accepted malaria as inevitable, but deliberate state action can control mosquitoes. Mosquitoes evolve to fit local weather and local human behaviour, so their traits change every 100-200 km. Control programmes therefore have to be designed neighbourhood by neighbourhood, and run by local people.
core_ideas.quote: It comes as a surprise to most people in India that actually mosquitoes can be controlled and purposive state action can actually make a huge difference to mosquito control.

core_ideas.explanation: Start at the lowest level of government and move a function up only when the lower level cannot handle it. Monetary policy belongs at the top, since changing currency at the Maharashtra-Gujarat border would be absurd. Mosquito control can be done by a village or a city, so it belongs there. In effect: decentralize by default and centralize only by exception.
core_ideas.quote: every function of government should be placed at the lowest level at which it can be done.

core_ideas.concept: The EU: Decide Function by Function, Not by Map
core_ideas.explanation: The European Union is deliberately not a country. It pools what benefits from scale, such as the euro and NATO defence, and leaves the rest local. Personal law in Catholic Portugal and Spain differs from secular Northern Europe. Small armies can even fold their tank units into Germany's.
core_ideas.quote: That don't draw lines on maps and then start defining the state by lines on maps.

core_ideas.concept: States Are the Confused Middle Tier
core_ideas.explanation: Some things clearly belong to the Union, like monetary policy, defence and foreign policy. Others clearly belong to cities, like mosquito control. Very little is best done at the state level. Ajay agrees with Amit's point that what really matters is Bombay and the Union government.
core_ideas.quote: What is optimally placed at the state level is extremely limited.

core_ideas.concept: Cities and Villages Are Different Problems
core_ideas.explanation: The 73rd and 74th Amendments treated village and city government as parallel reforms. But a village of about 150 households, or 600 people, lacks the scale for enough civil servants, enough political competition, or real checks and balances. Research finds only weak gains from decentralizing to villages. Cities like Bombay, which has more people than Australia, have the scale to run things like a public health department, so they should be on 'the highway to greater decentralization.'
core_ideas.quote: I'm not a romantic about village level government.

core_ideas.concept: The Concurrent List Belongs to the Union, and Schemes Take the Rest
core_ideas.explanation: The Constitution sets out Union, State and Concurrent lists. The framers imagined the Concurrent list as a field for cooperation between the centre and states, but once the Union legislates on a concurrent subject, its law prevails. Planners in the early Planning Commission era then went after the State list through centrally sponsored schemes. The Union offers to pay, for example, 65% if a state runs education its way, which captures the state's own 35% and imposes the centre's design. Ajay wants these schemes abolished, the Concurrent list vacated by the Union, and a separate city list.
core_ideas.quote: And the concurrent list is a fantasy where the wise, capable chief minister of Maharashtra is supposed to be in a conversation with Jawaharlal Nehru and they will find a middle road in a collaborative way.

core_ideas.concept: A Slice of GST for Cities
core_ideas.explanation: Every GST transaction can be traced to the city where it happened. When Kelkar, Arbind Modi and Ajay drafted the GST blueprint for the FRBM implementation task force set up by Jaswant Singh in 2003, they saw that a city slice was possible. Of a roughly 10% single-rate GST, Ajay suggests about 3% to the Union, 2% to the state and 5% to the city. That would give cities their own revenue instead of depending on two finance commissions. State finance commissions are often never set up, lack technical capacity, and don't even pretend to be neutral. Property tax helps, but it can't raise enough.
core_ideas.quote: And currently cities are often like sitting as a supplicant at the end of two groups, and we hope that the two groups will each be fair and sound, and that may or may not be the case.

core_ideas.concept: Power and Accountability Are Disconnected in Indian Cities
core_ideas.explanation: Amit relays Shruti Rajagopalan's diagnosis. City residents can vote out municipal officials who have little power. The officials who do have power sit in state governments and depend on voters elsewhere. Governance stays bad because the lever residents can pull isn't attached to anything.
core_ideas.quote: the governance is going to be bad because power and accountability are not linked.

core_ideas.concept: Migration Means People Choosing Better Governments
core_ideas.explanation: Drawing on Hirschman's idea of 'exit' and James C. Scott's point that early states competed for people rather than land, Ajay celebrates migration. People sort themselves by values and move away from badly run places, whether from UP to the south or from Afghanistan and Syria to Europe. Life in most urban slums is better than in most villages, or people wouldn't move, so lamenting migration is a luxury belief. Migration also offsets falling birth rates in states that have gone through the demographic transition. Amit's caveat is that the incentive stays weak while tax money goes to the centre rather than the place a migrant moves to.
core_ideas.quote: And ultimately what matters is people, not territory.

core_ideas.concept: A Choice Between Bad and Bad
core_ideas.explanation: Decentralization sounds good in theory but runs into Indian reality. Chief ministers hold close to dictatorial power. State legislatures pass whatever the ruling party wants, with no equivalent of the Rajya Sabha forcing negotiation, and state judiciaries are often cowed. Keeping power in New Delhi means distant, unaccountable officials. Moving it down means local strongmen. Anyone who argues for decentralization also has to push for political reform at state and city level so that power is dispersed there too.
core_ideas.quote: my concern is that a chief minister in India is a little bit of a dictator.

core_ideas.concept: Growth Follows From Becoming a Republic
core_ideas.explanation: This is the argument of Kelkar and Shah's In Service of the Republic. A republic disperses power among executive, legislature and judiciary, and their conflicts are healthy because they keep each other in check. In this view, India's poverty and weak growth come from concentrated power and an overbearing Union. The same reasoning applies to states and cities, which need checks and balances rather than autocratic chief ministers or mayors.
core_ideas.quote: If you get the checks and balances, if you get a sensible republic, then the economic growth will inevitably follow.

core_ideas.concept: Every Government Needs Its Own Knowledge Community
core_ideas.explanation: Without data, researchers, published papers and public criticism, a government becomes nothing more than a contest for power. Real decentralization therefore needs knowledge communities at state and city level. Ajay's friends at Janaagraha suggest organizing them around 63 groups of similar cities, for example treating Bombay, New Bombay and Thane as one group with shared data and research.
core_ideas.quote: Every state requires a commensurate intellectual community.

core_ideas.concept: A Hundred States, Many of Them Cities
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's rule of thumb is that India should have about 100 states, and many of them should be cities. Calcutta, for instance, could be split off from West Bengal as a full state. It would then deal directly with the Finance Commission and could receive a share of GST. Doing this within the existing constitutional framework avoids risky constitutional amendments at a time when drafting capability is poor.
core_ideas.quote: So you know my thumb rule for India is we should be a hundred states. Okay, and many of the states should be cities and that would really improve a lot of things.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Ajay's ominous opening: 'Amit has a hungry look. Such men are dangerous.' Later he reveals the hunger is real: 'You've just woken up. You are fasting. I promise to make it worse.'
After Ajay's mosquito discussion, which ended on Ladakh, Amit says 'Mosquitoes and Ladakh' would be 'an incredible title for a rock album, a heavy metal album in fact.'

The running tank gag. Amit: 'You can never resist talking about tanks. Fine, Ajay Shah, one more time let's talk about tanks.' He then pictures a thumbnail of Ajay looking out of a tank, and signs off the episode with 'Ajay in a tank.'
Ajay voices the post-war Dutch attitude to Germany: 'Okay, fine, we forgive you, you know, we know you invaded us a couple of times, but we let it go.' Then they go back to buying German tanks.

The dog-bite story. Ajay: 'a series of wonderful things happened.' Amit: 'Starting with the biting.' Susan insists it was her fault: 'I was troubling the dog. So I mean it is fair that the dog bit me.' Ajay: 'Susan has like very high standards for good behavior.'

Vasant Dhar's friend Bubba claims to know everyone in the world. Trump's secretary welcomes him at Trump Tower. Biden spots him from the Oval Office and runs out, falling a couple of times on the way. At a packed Vatican festival, the Pope comes out on the balcony with Bubba beside him, and the man next to Vasant asks: 'Excuse me, who's that guy with Bubba?'
Amit on where state governments fit: when T20 cricket arrived, people said Test cricket will stay and T20 will stay, so who needs ODIs? 'So I think states are kinda like ODIs.'

Amit once worked out that Iceland's population equals that of Varsova, a Mumbai neighbourhood. Ajay: 'And half of them are fishermen.' Amit: 'Iceland or Varsova?' Ajay: 'Iceland.' Amit: 'But yeah, we have fishermen too and we are proud of them.'

As Amit starts the monkey-and-cats fable, Ajay notes: 'In this episode we've got a dog, a cat, a monkey.' Amit adds: 'And tanks, many, many tanks.' He also assures viewers the camera won't pan down, since there's no bread under this table.

Amit thanks Ajay for picking up his phone while saying 'mobile phone': 'I must thank you from the bottom of my heart for assuming that I am as stupid as I am... now I know what a mobile phone looks like.'

From Shruti Rajagopalan's talk on how Nehru amended the Constitution whenever he wanted to do something unconstitutional, Amit recalls an early cartoon. A reader asks the Parliament bookshop for a copy of the Constitution and is told: 'I'm sorry, we don't stock periodicals.'

Amit says there are two Ajay Shahs: 'a serious analytical mind, a man of history' and 'a heretic who thinks mad ideas and all of those mad ideas make sense.' He protests against the sober one and demands 'that the heretic present himself.'

A bee circles Amit mid-recording: 'It seems to have fallen in love with me, and while my charms are undoubted, I would not welcome this particular attention.' The hosts connect it to the song lyric behind their first episode's title, whose preceding line is 'Dragonflies are busy buzzing me.'
When Ajay suggests splitting West Bengal into two or three states, one of them Calcutta, Amit offers names: 'Calcutta, West and Bengal.'
Ajay says Bimal Patel is 'building a book.' Amit: 'I love the way you combine unexpected verbs and nouns, like in a previous episode you said solving a mountain.'
Ajay's jab at the Constitution's colonial roots: 'It is remarkable how much a plagiarism test would pick up things in the constitution of India that come from the Government of India Act' of 1935.

B.R. Ambedkar's argument for centralizing power: 'what is a village but a sink of localism, a den of ignorance and narrow mindedness.' Amit cites it as the strongest case against romanticizing village government, given caste and the treatment of women.

The 73rd and 74th Amendments came about when Rajiv Gandhi's INC had enough strength to amend the Constitution, with Mani Shankar Aiyar leading the push for a more decentralized India. Ajay argues the amendments 'did not remotely go far enough.'
